newsitem.title: UK: Banks shrug off talk of big equity options losses.
newsitem.headline: Banks shrug off talk of big equity options losses.

text.p: Investment banks denied on Monday that they are smarting from sharp losses after a surge in British share prices caught them short on certain derivative deals for retail investment products.

Insurance companies and other fund management groups which offer stock market-related investment bonds to private investors have been buying equity call (buy) options from the banks to underwrite their investment products linked to the performance of the FTSE-100 share index.

Market sources say overall losses amount to anything between 50 million and 350 million pounds ($84 million and $588 million) but the banks remain cool to these attempts to put a figure to the alleged losses.

"Speculation about potential losses -- even at the lower end -- is considerably overstated," said a spokesman at Union Bank of Switzerland. He would not comment on whether the bank had fully hedged its exposure in these products -- by buying futures contracts in the FTSE-100 index of leading British shares.
BZW, the investment banking arm of Barclays Bank, declined to comment on market speculation that it too has suffered losses.
"This is rumour and speculation. We never comment on our trading," said a BZW spokesman.
UBS and BZW figure among a number of banks which have been offering derivative deals for index-related investment products.
The derivatives are bought to protect the fund managers selling the investment product -- a type of long-term bond -- from losses if share prices rise.
To measure the movement of share prices, the FTSE-100 index is usually chosen as this gives a reading of UK share prices -- less dividends -- of Britain's 100 biggest companies.

Investment products under this category do not allow fund managers to sell securities -- shares and options -- that they do not already own and this usually restricts their equity derivatives involvement to buying call options.

In general, a call option allows the buyer to buy shares at an agreed price by a certain date in the future but it is not an obligation to buy the shares. This is in contrast to a futures contract which, if held to expiry, requires the buyer to "buy" the market.
Options in the off-exchange over-the-counter (OTC) market are used because they can be tailored to any requirement such as unusually long investment periods.

Usually, around 30 percent of the investment amount is earmarked to buy call options. The remainder is used to acquire commercial paper -- or corporate debt -- from banks and building societies in order to retain the capital value of the investment.

But tax changes announced in the national budget last month whereby the 20 percent tax credit on dividends was abolished for pension funds and companies meant that for every 80-pence net dividend paid to a company it could no longer claim the 20p tax credit which would have boosted its dividend income.
And this in turn has affected the value of call options because of the way these are priced.

The tax changes have lowered the stream of dividend income flows for the future so that the value of call options has had to be raised -- and this has been to the benefit of fund management groups but not the banks who are sellers of these options.
The problem for the banks has been compounded further by the unexpected rally in the stock market following the British budget.
But the banks say they have not put up the shutters on such deals and they are still taking on new business in this area.
